name: Gate Studios
text: Your train passes the site of Gate Studios, on the train's {side}, one of the studios known together as Elstree Studios. A single large stage was built here in Station Road in 1928; J. Arthur Rank bought it in 1950, renamed it Gate Studios and made religious films, the last of them John Wesley in 1954. The building was demolished in 2006 for new homes.

name: British Library
text: Your train passes near the British Library, on the train's {side}, the national library of the United Kingdom, with around 14 million books among more than 200 million items. Its purpose-built home beside St Pancras station was opened by Elizabeth II on June 25th 1998 and is a Grade I listed building.

name: Smithfield Market
text: Your train passes near Smithfield Market, on the train's {side}, London's only remaining wholesale market, where meat has been traded since medieval times. Its Victorian halls were designed by Sir Horace Jones, who also designed the Billingsgate and Leadenhall markets; the central market was finished in November 1868.

name: The Black Friar, Blackfriars
text: Your train passes the Black Friar, on the train's {side}, a pub built in about 1875 on the site of a medieval Dominican friary and remodelled in the Arts and Crafts style from 1905, with decoration on monastic themes by the sculptors Frederick T. Callcott and Henry Poole. Threatened with demolition in the 1960s, it was saved by a campaign led by Sir John Betjeman.

name: Blackfriars Railway Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Thames on Blackfriars Railway Bridge, opened in 1886 as St Paul's Railway Bridge. Blackfriars station's platforms now stretch across it under a roof of solar panels, the largest of only three solar bridges in the world; the row of columns beside it is all that remains of the first bridge, of 1864.

name: Michael Faraday Memorial
text: Your train passes near the Michael Faraday Memorial, on the train's {side}, a stainless steel box built in 1961 at Elephant and Castle, near the scientist's birthplace in Newington Butts. Inside is an electricity substation for the Northern and Bakerloo lines, a fitting tribute to a pioneer of electricity; it was listed in 1996.

name: Battersea Power Station
text: Your train passes near Battersea Power Station, on the train's {side}, one of the world's largest brick buildings, designed with Giles Gilbert Scott among its architects. Built in two halves between 1929 and 1955, with its four famous chimneys, it stopped generating in 1983 and stood empty until 2014; it now holds homes, shops, restaurants and offices.

name: Battersea Dogs & Cats Home
text: Your train passes near Battersea Dogs & Cats Home, on the train's {side}, one of the UK's oldest animal rescue centres. Mary Tealby started it in her scullery in Holloway in 1860 as “The Temporary Home for Lost and Starving Dogs”; it moved here in 1871, and has taken in cats since 1883.

name: Longhedge Railway Works
text: Your train passes the site of Longhedge Railway Works, on the train's {side}, built by the London, Chatham and Dover Railway on part of Long Hedge farm to serve its new terminus at Victoria. Its first workshops were finished in 1862, and locomotives and carriages were built and repaired here until the mid-1950s.

name: Grosvenor Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Thames on Grosvenor Bridge, the first railway bridge across the river in central London, opened in 1860 to carry two tracks into Victoria. Widened in 1865 and 1907, and rebuilt in the 1960s as ten bridges side by side, it now carries nine tracks.

name: 575 Wandsworth Road
text: Your train passes near 575 Wandsworth Road, on the train's {side}, a small Georgian terraced house bought in 1981 by the Kenyan poet Khadambi Asalache. For 20 years he covered its rooms in Moorish-style fretwork, cut by hand from discarded pine doors and boxes, and he left it to the National Trust, which now shows it on guided tours.

name: Brixton Academy
text: Your train passes near Brixton Academy, on the train's {side}, opened in 1929 as the Astoria cinema and theatre, and a concert hall since 1983. The Smiths played their last gig here in December 1986, and it has won the NME's award for best venue 12 times since 1994.

name: London Necropolis railway station
text: Your train passes near the old London Necropolis station, on the train's {side}, where from 1854 coffins and mourners left by train for Brookwood Cemetery in Surrey. Its second station, used from 1902, saw its last funeral train on April 11th 1941; its office building on Westminster Bridge Road still stands.

name: Hungerford Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Thames on Hungerford Bridge, which carried Isambard Kingdom Brunel's suspension footbridge from 1845 until the railway replaced it in 1864. Brunel's brick buttresses are still in use, and the old bridge's chains were reused in Bristol's Clifton Suspension Bridge.

name: The Old Vic
text: Your train passes near the Old Vic, on the train's {side}, a theatre opened in 1818 as the Royal Coburg Theatre. Under Lilian Baylis it staged Shakespeare from 1914, and from 1963 it was the first home of the National Theatre, under Laurence Olivier, until the company moved to the South Bank in 1976.

name: Teddington Cemetery
text: Your train passes Teddington Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1879 partly on a former orchard; some of its cherry trees are probably the orchard's last. It has many tall old trees, among them cedar, giant redwood and a large monkey puzzle, and the war graves of 70 Commonwealth service personnel.

name: Chapel in the Wood, Strawberry Hill
text: Your train passes near the Chapel in the Wood, on the train's {side}, built from 1772 to 1774 for Horace Walpole in the grounds of his home, Strawberry Hill House. An early example of the Gothic Revival, with a front of Portland stone based on a tomb in Salisbury Cathedral, it now stands in the grounds of St Mary's University.

name: Drayton Green railway station
text: Drayton Green station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1905 as Drayton Green Halt, named after a nearby park and open space. In the Office of Rail and Road's estimates for the years 2021 to 2023 it was the least used station in Greater London.

name: St Mary's Catholic Cemetery, Kensal Green
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Catholic Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1858 next door to Kensal Green Cemetery and now the resting place of more than 165,000 Roman Catholics. The nurse Mary Seacole and the conductor Sir John Barbirolli are buried here.

name: North Pole Depot
text: Your train passes near North Pole depot, on the train's {side}, on land that was once the northern part of Wormwood Scrubs. Eurostar kept its London trains here from 1994 to 2007, and from 2013 it was rebuilt to look after Great Western Railway's Hitachi trains.

name: Frestonia
text: Your train passes near Freston Road, on the train's {side}, where squatters facing eviction declared the Free and Independent Republic of Frestonia on October 31st 1977, and applied to join the United Nations. The actor David Rappaport was its Foreign Minister, and in 1982 the Clash recorded their album Combat Rock at a studio here.

name: Willesden Traction Maintenance Depot
text: Your train passes Willesden depot, on the train's {side}, opened in March 1965 to look after the new electric locomotives of the West Coast Main Line. Its six shed roads each hold four locomotives; since 2016 it has looked after the Class 710 electric trains.

name: Lots Road Power Station
text: Your train passes near Lots Road Power Station, on the train's {side}, built on Chelsea Creek to power the District Railway, which let its trains change from steam to electric. It began generating on February 1st 1905, and powered the Underground until it was switched off on October 21st 2002, after 97 years.

name: Shaftesbury Park Estate
text: Your train passes the Shaftesbury Park Estate, on the train's {side}, built in the 1870s by the Artizans, Labourers and General Dwellings Company to give working people decent homes. Lord Shaftesbury laid its foundation stone on August 3rd 1872, giving it its name, and the reformers behind it made sure it had no pub.

name: Chelsea Bridge
text: Your train passes near Chelsea Bridge, on the train's {side}, opened in 1937 on the site of an ancient ford. The first self-anchored suspension bridge in Britain, built entirely with materials from the British Empire, it replaced a toll bridge of 1858.

name: Grosvenor Canal
text: Your train passes near the Grosvenor Canal, on the train's {side}, opened in 1824 and cut back as the railway into Victoria, and then housing, were built over it. Barges loaded with the city's refuse used it until 1995, making it the last canal in Greater London in commercial use; a small part survives.

name: St Paul's Church, Clapham
text: Your train passes near St Paul's Church, Clapham, on the train's {side}, on a site with a church since the 12th century. The present building, in a plain classical style by Christopher Edmonds, was finished in 1815; its churchyard has many early 19th-century tombs and a community garden called Eden.

name: Clapham Grand
text: Your train passes near the Grand, on the train's {side}, which opened on St John's Hill on November 26th 1900 as the New Grand Theatre of Varieties, built for a group led by the music hall stars Dan Leno and Herbert Campbell. After years as a cinema and a bingo club, it is now a nightclub, music venue and theatre.

name: Latchmere Recreation Ground (Brown Dog statue)
text: Your train passes near Latchmere Recreation Ground, on the train's {side}, where a bronze statue of a brown terrier was unveiled in 1906 in protest at experiments on live animals. It caused such controversy that the council removed it in 1910; a new brown dog statue was put up in Battersea Park in 1985.

name: Embassy of the United States, London
text: Your train passes near the Embassy of the United States, on the train's {side}, the largest American embassy in western Europe. It moved here to Nine Elms from Grosvenor Square, where the embassy had been since 1938, and opened to the public on December 13th 2017.

name: New Covent Garden Market
text: Your train passes near New Covent Garden Market, on the train's {side}, the largest wholesale fruit, vegetable and flower market in the United Kingdom. It moved here from Covent Garden on the site of the old Nine Elms locomotive depot, opening on November 11th 1974; its fruit and vegetable traders work from about midnight to 6am.

name: Rainbow Theatre
text: Your train passes the Rainbow Theatre, on the train's {side}, built in 1930 as the Finsbury Park Astoria, an “atmospheric” cinema with a Spanish-Moorish fantasy of an interior. It was here, on March 31st 1967, that Jimi Hendrix first set fire to his guitar on stage; it later became a famous music venue.

name: Keskidee Centre
text: Your train passes near the former Keskidee Centre, on the train's {side}, Britain's first arts centre for the Black community, opened in 1971 by the Guyanese architect Oscar Abrams in an old mission hall in Gifford Street. In 1978 Bob Marley made a video here for “Is This Love”, with a seven-year-old Naomi Campbell among the children.

name: Camley Street Natural Park
text: Your train passes Camley Street Natural Park, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve run by the London Wildlife Trust on a narrow strip beside the Regent's Canal at St Pancras Lock. Its wetland, meadow and woodland have more than 300 kinds of higher plants, including the common spotted orchid.

name: Kings Cross Top Shed
text: Your train passes the site of King's Cross Top Shed, on the train's {side}, the Great Northern Railway's engine shed for London, opened in 1850 on the far side of the Regent's Canal from the station. Its gently curved main running shed had 25 roads; the depot closed in June 1963 and was soon demolished.

name: Gasworks Tunnel
text: Your train runs through the Gasworks Tunnel, just outside King's Cross, which carries the East Coast Main Line under the Regent's Canal in three bores opened between 1852 and 1892. The eastern bore was taken out of use in 1977 and brought back in 2021 to give the line more room.

name: Reedham railway station (London)
text: Your train passes Reedham station, on the train's {side}, on the Tattenham Corner line beside this one, opened as Reedham Halt on March 1st 1911. It is named after the Reedham Asylum for Fatherless Children, founded by the philanthropist Andrew Reed in 1844, which later became Reedham School and closed in 1980.

name: Streatham Hill Theatre
text: Your train passes near Streatham Hill Theatre, on the train's {side}, opened in 1929, the last theatre designed by W. G. R. Sprague. It staged plays, opera, ballet and variety until 1962 and was then a bingo hall until 2017; listed as an unusually lavish theatre of its time, it is on Historic England's Heritage at Risk register.

name: South London Theatre
text: Your train passes near the South London Theatre, on the train's {side}, a community theatre in a Gothic Revival fire station built in 1881 for horse-drawn engines, with its look-out tower and doors still in place. Motor fire engines were too big for the doors, so it closed as a fire station in 1917; the first play opened here in October 1967.

name: Platforms Piece
text: Your train passes Platforms Piece, on the train's {side}, bronze statues of commuters on Brixton station by Kevin Atherton, unveiled by Sir Hugh Casson on June 30th 1986. Atherton modelled them on three Brixton people, Peter Lloyd, Joy Battick and Karin Heistermann; a fourth figure, Joy II, was added in 2023.
